liptay1968.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache
liptay1968.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968.venue: IBM Systems Journal, Vol. 7, No. 1, pp. 15-21 (as printed on the article: "IBM SYSTEMS JOURNAL · VOL. 7 · NO. 1 · 1968")
liptay1968.quote: However, it is not feasible to provide a large main storage with an access time commensurate with the 80-nanosecond processor cycle of the Model 85. ... The storage hierarchy consists of a 1.04-microsecond main storage and a small, fast store called a cache, which is integrated into the CPU. The cache is not addressable by a program, but rather is used to hold the contents of those portions of main storage that are currently being used.
supports: 80-nanosecond processor cycle
1.04-microsecond main storage
the cache is not addressable by a program
page 15

liptay1968size.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — Cache organization (p. 16)
liptay1968size.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968size.quote: The main storage units that can be used on the Model 85 are the IBM 2365-5 and the 2385. They have a 1.04-microsecond cycle time and make available capacities from 512K bytes to 4096K bytes (K = 1024). The cache is a 16K-byte integrated storage, which is capable of operating every processor cycle. Optionally, it can be expanded to 24K bytes or 32K bytes.
supports: 16K-byte cache
main storage 512K to 4096K bytes
24K and 32K options

liptay1968compat.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — the compatibility requirement (p. 15)
liptay1968compat.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968compat.quote: When the program starts operating on data in a different portion of main storage, the data in that portion must be loaded into the cache and the data from some other portion removed. This activity must take place without program assistance, since the Model 85 must be compatible with the rest of the SYSTEM/360 line.
supports: loading and discarding happen without program assistance
compatibility with the rest of the System/360 line is the stated reason

liptay1968store.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — store operations (p. 17)
liptay1968store.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968store.quote: Store operations always cause main storage to be updated. If the main storage sector being changed has a cache sector assigned to it, the cache is also updated; otherwise, no activity related to the cache takes place.
supports: store-through: no write lands only in the cache

liptay1968evict.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — why eviction is free (p. 17)
liptay1968evict.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968evict.quote: Since all of the data in the cache is also in main storage, it is not necessary on a cache sector reassignment to move any data from the cache to main storage. All that is required is to change the sector address register, reset the validity bits, and initiate loading of a block.
supports: any entry may be discarded at any moment and the machine stays correct
the validity bit

liptay1968channel.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — channels (p. 18)
liptay1968channel.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968channel.quote: Channel fetches are processed by getting the required data from main storage without referring to the cache. Channel stores are handled the same way as processor stores. In this way, if a channel changes data that is in the cache, the cache is updated but the channels do not have any part of the cache devoted to them.
supports: a second writer into main storage has to be routed through the cache
channel stores follow the processor store path

liptay1968hit.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — performance studies (pp. 18-19)
liptay1968hit.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968hit.quote: Figure 4 shows the distribution of this probability for the same 19 trace tapes used for Figure 3. The average probability was 0.968. It is worth noting that, if the addresses generated by a program were random, the probability of finding the data wanted in the cache would be much less than 0.01. Therefore, it can be said that what makes the cache work is the fact that real programs are not random in their addressing patterns.
supports: 19 trace tapes
average hit probability 0.968 (simulated, not measured on hardware)
much less than 0.01 on random addresses
the closing sentence of the performance section

liptay1968name.title: Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache — cited reference and footnote (p. 21)
liptay1968name.author: J. S. Liptay
liptay1968name.quote: 1. The term cache is synonymous with high-speed buffer, as used in other Model 85 documentation.
supports: the word 'cache' is introduced in this paper as a synonym for IBM's internal term 'high-speed buffer'

ca1968census.title: Monthly Computer Census (figures as of February 15, 1968), Computers and Automation, March 1968, p. 63
ca1968census.author: Computers and Automation (Berkeley Enterprises)
ca1968census.quote: AS OF FEBRUARY 15, 1968 ... IBM (N) White Plains, N.Y. ... 360/67 $138,000 10/66 ... 360/75 $81,400 2/66 ... 360/85 $158,000 [dash under DATE OF FIRST INSTALLATION] 0 [NUMBER OF INSTALLATIONS] [columns: NAME OF COMPUTER | AVERAGE OR RANGE OF MONTHLY RENTAL | DATE OF FIRST INSTALLATION | NUMBER OF INSTALLATIONS]. Legend, p. 62: "(N) - manufacturer refuses to give any figures on number of installations or of orders"; the census itself is "a summary made by 'Computers and Automation' of reports and estimates".
supports: $158,000 listed as the 360/85 average monthly rental in the March 1968 census (figures as of February 15, 1968)
a dash under date of first installation and 0 installations for the 360/85
$138,000 for the 360/67 and $81,400 for the 360/75 on the same page

ca1968news.title: IBM Announces Powerful System/360, Model 85 (Newsletter), Computers and Automation, March 1968, p. 55
ca1968news.author: Computers and Automation (Berkeley Enterprises)
ca1968news.quote: Another feature is compatibility among System/360 models. Programs written for other large-scale System/360s will operate faster in the Model 85 without modification. ... First customer shipments will be scheduled for the third quarter of 1969.
supports: compatibility was sold as a headline feature
first customer shipments scheduled for Q3 1969

unverified: That the Model 85 was designed at IBM Poughkeepsie. Plausible and widely repeated, but no primary source opened for this chapter states it, so no place name appears in the story.

That the Model 85 was the first commercially available machine with a cache. IBM's own history page claims 'the first in the industry' and Wikipedia repeats it; that is a vendor claim and no primary source opened here supports it, so the story does not say 'first'.
The exact announcement date in January 1968. Only the March 1968 trade reporting was opened.

That IBM Systems Journal editor Lyle R. Johnson suggested the word 'cache'. Attributed to Pugh, Johnson and Palmer's 'IBM's 360 and Early 370 Systems' (1991), which was not opened. Only Liptay's own footnote is used.
Purchase price, as opposed to monthly rental. The census lists rental only.

Whether the $158,000 figure is IBM's own list rental. IBM is marked (N) in the census - it refused to give figures - so the row is Computers and Automation's summary of reports and estimates, and no Model 85 was installed at the time for anyone to have paid it.

Whether the 0.968 hit probability and the 81-percent-of-ideal figure hold on shipped hardware. Both are trace-driven simulation results in Liptay's paper; the Model 85 had not shipped when they were published.
